**Yes, the cable can cap your charging speed.** Charging runs at the lowest limit among the charger, the device, and the cable.

**What each rating means**
- **60W (3A at 20V):** Standard USB-C cables carry up to 3A, and they don't need an e-marker chip. A 60W cable is enough for phones, tablets, and many ultrabooks.
- **100W (5A at 20V):** This needs a cable with an e-marker chip that advertises 5A. USB-IF says 100W USB-C to USB-C cables were replaced by 240W cables in the Type-C 2.1 spec, and it stopped certifying new 100W cables on December 22, 2021 ([UL Solutions](https://www.ul.com/insights/240w-usb-c-cable-performance-testing-and-safety-considerations)). Uncertified 100W cables are still sold. For example, one Baseus listing is e-marked at 5A but explicitly not rated for 140W or 240W.
- **240W (5A at 48V, "EPR"):** This requires an e-marker and the 240W logo. The Power Delivery 3.1 spec adds 28V, 36V and 48V levels, which give up to 140W, 180W and 240W ([USB-IF](https://www.usb.org/usb-charger-pd)).

**Other points**
- Certified USB-C to USB-C cables must carry either a 60W or a 240W power logo ([USB-IF](https://www.usb.org/cable_connector)). Look for that mark.
- A better cable can't add power. USB-IF notes that a certified cable doesn't augment the capabilities of the products it connects ([USB-IF](https://www.usb.org/cable_connector)).
- Power rating and data speed are separate. A cable can be rated for 100W or 240W and still be limited to USB 2.0 data (480 Mbps).

**What to buy**
- **Device uses 60W or less:** Any decent 60W cable works.
- **Device uses 65–100W:** Get a 5A e-marked cable.
- **Device uses more than 100W (some gaming laptops):** Get a 240W cable, and make sure your charger supports the higher voltages.
